interest: This document is particularly interesting to economic and diplomatic historians as it reflects a notable shift in the mid-1930s regarding Japanese technological development and intellectual property. While pre-war Japan was frequently stereotyped in the West as an imitator or infringer of foreign patents, Sub-number 19 highlights Japanese authorities' growing concern over foreign 'pirating' of Japanese domestic industrial technique and the deployment of military police (gendarmerie / Kempeitai) to investigate foreign commercial inquiries. Furthermore, Sub-number 20 demonstrates that U.S. consular officials such as Richard F. Boyce were actively tracking Japan's indigenous inventive capacity and recognizing it as an increasingly formidable factor in international trade on the eve of the Second World War.
overview: This file consists of a single docket sheet (List of Papers, designated Page #2) for State Department decimal file 894.54, which covers Japanese literary, artistic, and industrial property, including laws governing patents, designs, trademarks, and utility models. The sheet indexes two consular documents received in 1936: Sub-number 19, a July 8 despatch from Consul General Arthur Garrels in Tokyo enclosing a Japan Advertiser clipping regarding the 'pirating' of Japanese industrial techniques and gendarmerie surveillance of foreign manufacturing inquiries; and Sub-number 20, a September 30 report from Consul Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama analyzing Japanese inventive capacity and its growing competitive impact on international commerce.

subfiles.summary: This list of papers (Page #2 of the docket for file 894.54) indexes communications relating to Japanese literary, artistic, and industrial property. It records Sub-number 19, a July 8, 1936 despatch from Arthur Garrels in Tokyo reporting on the pirating of Japanese industrial technique and gendarmerie countermeasures against foreign inquiries, enclosing an article from the Japan Advertiser. It also records Sub-number 20, a September 30, 1936 report by Richard F. Boyce in Yokohama examining Japanese inventive capacity and its impact on international trade.
